question: How visual cues override our sense of taste and smell, demonstrated by a 2001 study where enology students described a dyed white wine as a red wine.

facts.fact: In 2001, Frédéric Brochet conducted a study as part of his dissertation on perception and wine tasting.
facts.quote: The study, conducted by Frédéric Brochet in 2001, was part of a larger dissertation on perception and wine tasting

facts.fact: The study investigated the interaction between the vision of colors and odor determination.
facts.quote: The interaction between the vision of colors and odor determination is investigated

facts.fact: A psychophysical experiment was performed involving a panel of 54 tasters.
facts.quote: A white wine artificially colored red with an odorless dye was olfactory described as a red wine by a panel of 54 tasters.

facts.fact: The tasters were given two identical white wines that differed only in color, and were asked to assign descriptors to them.
facts.quote: So they were given two identical white wines, different only in color, and asked to assign them descriptors from both red and white wines.

facts.fact: Most of the people assigned the red descriptors to the white wine that had been artificially colored red.
facts.quote: With no other difference between them, and being required to assign the red descriptors to one of the wines, most people assigned them to the red-colored wine instead of randomly.

facts.fact: The researchers concluded that because of the visual information, the tasters discounted the actual olfactory information.
facts.quote: Hence, because of the visual information, the tasters discounted the olfactory information.

facts.fact: The story is frequently retold claiming that 'wine experts' were completely fooled, but the subjects were actually undergraduate enology students.
facts.quote: -The most important is that the subjects in this experiment were not, in fact 'wine experts'. They were undergraduate enology students.

facts.fact: It is a myth that every single person was oblivious to the trick.
facts.quote: - It's simply not true that “Every single one, all 54, could not tell it was white.” as is frequently stated.

facts.fact: Some people did correctly give white wine descriptions to the dyed-red wine.
facts.quote: the paper that is frequently cited shows that indeed some people gave 'white wine' descriptions to the dyed-red wine.

people.name: Frédéric Brochet
people.role: Researcher and author of the dissertation
people.stake: Discovering if visual cues could override a trained sense of smell for his dissertation on wine perception

people.name: 54 Enology Students
people.role: Undergraduate wine science students acting as the tasting panel
people.stake: Their ability to accurately evaluate the smells of wine utilizing their specific training

timeline.what: Frédéric Brochet designed a psychophysical experiment for his dissertation with 54 undergraduate enology students.
timeline.why: To investigate the interaction between the vision of colors and odor determination.

timeline.what: Brochet served the students two identical white wines, but one was artificially dyed red, and asked them to describe the wines.
timeline.why: To test if their visual perception of a red color would make them use red wine descriptors despite smelling white wine.

timeline.what: The findings showed that most students assigned red descriptors to the dyed white wine.
timeline.why: Because their perception was hijacked by visual information, causing them to discount their olfactory senses.

turn.what: The moment the trained enology students confidently described a white wine using red-wine terms because it was dyed red, proving that sight overrides smell.

key_objects: Two glasses of identical white wine
A white wine artificially dyed red
Tasting notes assigning red wine descriptors to white wine
unverified: The subjects were widely reported as 'wine experts' or seasoned professionals, but they were actually undergraduate wine science students [f7].
Popular retellings claim every single one of the 54 students was completely oblivious to the trick, but some actually did use white wine descriptors [f8, f9].
